Watch: Huge waves pummel northeast US as storm barrels through
Tens of millions of people across the north-eastern US are in the path of a powerful storm bringing coastal flooding, power cuts, travel chaos and cancelled stadium events.
The so-called nor'easter is bringing "dangerous coastal flooding and beach conditions, strong winds and heavy rainfall" to areas including New York City and Boston on Saturday, the US National Weather Service (NWS) said.
States of emergency have been declared in New York and New Jersey, both of which faced a coastal deluge in some areas. Rain and strong winds are forecast from Virginia to Maine.
In Brooklyn, a man was killed by a falling tree, the BBC's US partner CBS News reported.
Surf City, New Jersey, was among coastal communities flooded
The nor'easter has caused widespread power cuts. More than 100,000 households, nearly all in the northeast US, have lost electricity, according to tracker PowerOutage.
The Federal Aviation Administration recommended air passengers check with airlines about their flight status. More than 2,400 flights have been delayed and another 1,199 grounded, according to FlightAware.
Saturday's full moon is projected to worsen coastal flooding. Streets and homes were inundated with floodwater in the coastal New Jersey communities of Surf City and Manasquan on Saturday.
"I urge all New Jerseyans to take this storm seriously, stay alert and follow local guidance," Governor Mikie Sherrill said.
Residents on kayaks in a Beach Haven West, New Jersey, neighbourhood
NWS said in its alert: "Prepare immediately for significant inundation in low-lying areas near the shore, including roads underwater and impacts to homes and businesses."
In New York, officials are warning of wind gusts of up to 55mph (86km/h) throughout the weekend, leading to downed trees and power lines.
"Don't travel if you don't have to," NYC Mayor Zohran Mamdani told residents in a video message. "Do not drive or walk through floodwater."
In the Boston area, the Red Sox moved the last game in their series against the Chicago Cubs to Sunday afternoon in Florida.
Streets and homes were inundated with floodwater in coastal parts of New Jersey
Flights have been delayed or cancelled due to the storm
A professional football match between Red Bull New York and St Louis City SC was also cancelled.
The Global Citizen Festival concert in New York City's Central Park, which was to be headlined by Lauryn Hill, Wyclef Jean and John Legend, will not go ahead.
Ed Sheeran's Boston concert was also among events called off due to the weather.
Sheeran's concert at the Gillette Stadium in the Boston area was cancelled for safety reasons, the venue said.

articles.title_orig: Host Jalen Brunson gets assist from Knicks on 'SNL' premiere
articles.title_zh: Host Jalen Brunson gets assist from Knicks on 'SNL' premiere
articles.content_orig:
Live from New York, it’s Knicks MVP Jalen Brunson.
Jalen Brunson once again made Knicks history as the first Big Apple basketball star from the franchise to host “Saturday Night Live.”
Brunson, who just turned 30 earlier this month, traded in his basketball skills for sketch comedy as he dazzled in the season 52 premiere of “SNL” featuring musical guest pop group Katseye on Saturday night.
Fresh off the back of his thrilling run to the NBA championship which ended the Knicks’ 53-year title drought, Brunson opened his monologue nonchalantly saying he had a “pretty good summer.”
“So the first three quarters of the show are gonna be god awful, but the last sketch is gonna be amazing,” Brunson joked, in a reference to the Knicks’ multiple Finals comebacks.
Brunson quipped about how he’s excited to return to the iconic Madison Square Garden for the upcoming NBA season in “the exact same spot where Taylor and Travis got married” in July.
The Knicks MVP poked fun at ESPN’s Stephen A. Smith, portrayed by “SNL” mainstay Kenan Thompson, joking that the broadcaster owes him an apology for questioning his ability to lead the team to the championship.
Fellow Knicks players, Josh Hart, OG Anunoby, Mikal Bridges and Karl-Anthony Towns were in the audience at 30 Rockefeller for Brunson’s hosting debut and later joined him on stage.
During his monologue, Brunson took audience questions from his fellow Championship-winning team members which included Bridges asking if his over 7 feet arm spam is long and if he really took a $113 million pay cut re-signing with the Knicks.
Towns fanboys over Brunson, claiming he is a “big fan,” but cheekily asks if he can “foul out of ‘SNL.’”
Brunson says no, prompting Towns to say, “so I could be here like the whole show? Nice,” earning a roaring ovation from the audience.
“OG” then asks Brunson, “Remember in game 4 when you took that shot at the end and you missed it” — referring to Brunson’s missed shot in San Antonio that was tipped in by Anunoby, ensuring the Knicks would win the game.
Brunson even put Hart on the spot, asking the shooting guard why he poked his thumb into his backside on live television while celebrating winning the NBA Cup in December 2025 which became a viral internet clip.
During the show, Knicks die-hard fan Ben Stiller took to X declaring Brunson’s monologue to be the “BEST MONOLOGUE EVER.”
In one sketch, Brunson broke out singing, flexing his vocals while dunking on the iconic Disney movie “High School Musical.”
In the final sketch of the night, Brunson is seen in the Knicks’ locker room when his third grade basketball coach sneaks in and praises how “proud of you I am” while joking about the biggest steak Brunson has ever eaten.
Brunson closed the show by saying he’s “Going to get back to my real job pretty soon” and was joined on stage by musical guest Katseye, who was decked out in Knicks jackets and hats.
The Knicks MVP is just the fifth NBA player to host in the show’s almost 51-year run — following in the footsteps of Bill Russell, Michael Jordan, LeBron James and three-time host Charles Barkley, according to a list compiled by Sporting News.
Brunson is also only the third athlete from a New York-based team to host the late-night show, joining former Giants great Eli Manning and Yankees Hall of Famer Derek Jeter.
Ahead of the nor’easter set to pummel the Big Apple, the first-time host surprised dedicated fans braving the elements Friday night trying to secure tickets inside the studio at 30 Rockefeller.
NBC pages handed out pricey Levain cookies to hopeful fans who must camp out in line from 7 p.m. to 12 a.m. the night before the show’s taping to receive a number, which may or may not get them into the studio for Saturday night.
“It was really, really nice. And I do believe that it actually came from him and his team and they were generous because I’m sure when he hears that people are sitting on the sidewalk, even with potential tickets, that’s a big deal,” Judson said.
The point guard made sure that everyone in the line, which extended beyond 100 people, was handed one of the famous New York City cookies — that cost $5.75 at Levain.

articles.title_orig: Trump rejects Iran’s seven-day roadmap to end war and reopen Hormuz
articles.title_zh: Trump rejects Iran’s seven-day roadmap to end war and reopen Hormuz
articles.content_orig:
Araghchi ignores Trump, waits for mediators’ response on Hormuz
United States President Donald Trump has rejected a plan submitted by Iran to reopen the Strait of Hormuz within seven days, as Tehran continued to insist that only diplomacy can solve the conflict between the two countries.
Speaking to reporters at the White House, Trump said on Saturday that Iran wants to make a deal to open the vital maritime corridor immediately only “because they are losing so badly”.
“They want to make a deal, and I think that’s fine. I’d like to make a deal, too,” he said. But the proposal put forth by Iran “would not be acceptable,” he said.
The plan by Iran, announced on Friday at the United Nations General Assembly, calls for the US to release frozen Iranian funds, lift oil sanctions and end its naval blockade on Iranian ports.
Abbas Araghchi, Iran’s foreign minister, said at the time that those steps could be completed within four or five days, clearing the way for the strait to reopen and for negotiations on a final agreement to begin by the seventh day.
Araghchi responded to Trump’s rejection in a post on his Telegram channel on Saturday, saying Iran “will not back down” on its conditions.
“We have seen the first reaction from the US president, but nothing has been conveyed to us from the mediators yet,” Araghchi wrote, adding that Trump had a history of making “contradictory” statements.
He said Iran was “waiting for the definitive opinions to be conveyed to us by the mediators” and would “make a decision based on that”. He added that “only a negotiated solution” can get the US “out of this deadlock”.
US officials had signalled on Friday that Trump would reject the proposal. The Wall Street Journal, citing unnamed US officials, reported that Trump was “privately sceptical” that Tehran would meet his demands. He reportedly told aides that he expects a renewed bombing campaign on Iran after the US midterm elections in November.
Al Jazeera’s Mike Hanna, reporting from Washington, DC, said the Iranian proposal appears “dead in the water”. But he noted Trump has offered no alternative.
“The one thing that has been made clear by President Trump is that he is content to stay in the status of limbo,” Hanna said, “despite concerns from much of the American public that the Iran conflict is turning into another ‘never-ending war’.”
Iran closed the Strait of Hormuz, a waterway critical to global oil supplies, shortly after the US and Israel launched their war on February 28. Iranian attacks on vessels in the waterway have since sharply curtailed shipping.
The US has responded with an economic blockade on Iran and threats of secondary sanctions against airports and companies doing business with Iranian airlines – measures that have already prompted the United Arab Emirates, Iraq and Oman to cancel flights .
Earlier in the week, Araghchi met with Steve Witkoff, Trump’s envoy, to lay out conditions for ending the war, which would also include waiving oil sanctions and establishing a regional ceasefire covering Lebanon and Yemen.
Iran’s President Masoud Pezeshkian, who was also in New York for the UNGA, said on Saturday that Tehran no longer trusted negotiations with Washington, citing past rounds of talks that were followed by military strikes and new sanctions.
“We have no trust in the American side and do not know on what basis an understanding can be reached with it,” Pezeshkian told Al Jazeera.
He denied that Iran bore responsibility for the closure of the strait, saying the US had “closed the routes before us”. He said the waterway would reopen to commercial shipping if negotiations succeeded in ending the war.
Ross Harrison, a senior fellow at the Middle East Institute, said Iran’s proposal was intended chiefly as a gesture of goodwill.
“I think they are trying to show the willingness to talk and negotiate,” he told Al Jazeera. “That’s what’s important for their home audience back in Iran, and it’s also important for the American public.”
Harrison said Iran’s leaders likely anticipated Trump’s rejection, since the proposal closely mirrored the now failed memorandum of understanding signed in June that Tehran believes Washington had undermined.
“I don’t think they were surprised at all” by Trump’s move, he said.

articles.title_orig: Trump Promotes Criticism of Republican Who Broke With Him on Immigration
articles.title_zh: Trump Promotes Criticism of Republican Who Broke With Him on Immigration
articles.content_orig:
Rep. Maria Elvira Salazar, R-Florida, has made waves by publicly breaking with President Donald Trump over immigration.
"Mr. President, some of your immigration enforcement efforts have gone too far," Salazar says in a new campaign ad . "The same Hispanics that helped you get to the White House in 2024 feel betrayed today."
In 2024, voters broadly trusted Republicans to handle illegal immigration. Through incompetence and cruelty, the Trump administration has lost that goodwill. The last election showed Republicans have a path forward on immigration. But to take it, they need to ditch the cruel memes and aggressive tactics that have plagued Trump's second term.
Salazar is right: Hispanics were a major part of Trump's 2024 victory. According to Pew Research Center, the president nearly tied former Vice President Kamala Harris among Hispanic voters, a group former President Joe Biden won by 25 percentage points in 2020.
Since then, Trump's gains among Hispanics have evaporated. In February 2025, according to Pew , 93% of Hispanics who voted for Trump approved of the job he was doing. By April of this year, just 66% did. Over the same stretch, his approval among all Hispanic adults fell from 36% to 22%, while among non-Hispanic adults, it slipped from 49% to 37%.
The drop in support can be attributed largely to the administration's mishandling of immigration.
The loudest headlines came out of Operation Metro Surge, the enforcement campaign that flooded Minneapolis with more than 3,000 federal agents last winter. The surge was driven more by political optics than by any strategic need, and it ended with Immigration and Customs Enforcement and Border Patrol agents shooting and killing two U.S. citizens, Renee Good and Alex Pretti.
Worse yet, administration officials then smeared Pretti . White House advisor Stephen Miller called him a "domestic terrorist," and the Department of Homeland Security claimed he "wanted to do maximum damage and massacre law enforcement." Bystander video showed he never drew his holstered pistol, which he was licensed to carry. Americans noticed: 61% of voters told Quinnipiac University pollsters that the administration had not given an honest account of the shooting.
Previously: We need to change the way we talk about the ICE shooting | Opinion
By mid-February, Americans opposed ICE's tactics 62% to 31%, according to an ABC News/Washington Post/Ipsos poll. The backlash presumably helped cost Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem her job.
Since Noem's firing, ICE has largely faded from the headlines, as DHS Sec. Markwayne Mullin has worked to keep the agency out of the spotlight. That changed Sept. 20, when an ICE officer in Austin shot and wounded Wilber Rafael Garcés Pérez, a Venezuelan man with a deportation order who had fled a vehicle stop. The facts are still unclear, and there is no ICE body-camera footage of the shooting. After Minneapolis, Americans have little reason to give the administration the benefit of the doubt.

Beyond the heated environment it needlessly created in Minnesota, the administration has driven support away with its messaging.
Throughout Trump's second term, official government social media accounts have churned out memes , many of them about immigration. The White House posted a Studio Ghibli-style cartoon of a convicted drug trafficker weeping as she was arrested and has promised that "the memes will continue." Other posts have included mock travel ads for deportation flights, and the administration has co-opted endless TikTok memes and audio trends to celebrate deportations.
All of it undercuts the administration's posture on such a serious matter. Nobody has ever been won over to a policy by a cartoon of a crying deportee, criminal or not. All it does is deepen the divide.
Austin ICE shooting proves we've lost ability to wait for facts | Opinion
Frustration with Democrats' failures at the border handed Republicans an opening in 2024. Voters trusted Trump over Harris on immigration 51% to 38%. Republicans have since squandered that advantage, but the path to a sensible immigration policy isn't closed.
An Immigration and Customs Enforcement officer shot and injured a man in North Austin on Sept. 20, officials say.
The man who was injured in the shooting was identified as Wilber Rafael Garces Perez, 28, of Venezuela, by Austin immigration lawyer Kate Lincoln-Goldfinch, who said she was hired to represent him.
The incident was followed by a swift reaction from elected officials, as the public protested the latest shooting involving federal officers in the United States this year.

Americans still draw a line between securing the border and Trump's broader crackdown. In a New York Times/Siena College poll in January, roughly half of voters approved of his handling of the border, while they were split on deportations and a clear majority said ICE had "gone too far." That gap shows sensible border policy still has broad support, despite the administration's spectacle of mismanagement and cruelty.
Trump's inroads with Hispanic voters in 2024 were thought to signal a new Republican coalition, and they showed that these voters could back a more conservative immigration policy. Those gains have all but vanished. What looked like a lasting Republican asset has become a serious liability heading into the midterms.
To win back their advantage on immigration, Republicans need to ditch the cruelty. The memes, ICE's aggressive tactics and the general callousness have soured Americans on policies that should command popular support for years to come.
Lawmakers like Salazar may be breaking with Trump for electoral reasons. But if they win in November, they will be the ones building the Republican Party's next approach to immigration. That approach should press Democrats on their weaknesses on the issue, without the cruelty that has defined Trump's second term.
Dace Potas, a law student, is an opinion columnist for USA TODAY. Follow him on X: @DacePotas .

articles.title_orig: OpenAI halts training of latest models as reports mount of AI agents going rogue
articles.title_zh: OpenAI halts training of latest models as reports mount of AI agents going rogue
articles.content_orig:
Decision follows disclosures that OpenAI agents searching government websites had acted in unexpected ways
OpenAI said it has paused training of its latest artificial intelligence models as reports of AI agents going rogue mount.
The decision to halt development came just hours after the company disclosed Friday that it was reviewing several incidents from the summer in which OpenAI agents searching federal government websites acted in unexpected ways beyond what was asked of them while gathering and distributing information.
Separately, the AI evaluator Transluce said agents that appeared to come from OpenAI tried unsuccessfully to hack into a US Department of Education website, a detail that OpenAI has not confirmed.
OpenAI said in a statement that it will resume training “only when we are confident that we have additional safeguards” in place, adding that it expects it will have to “hit pause” again as AI develops and other issues emerge.
Last week Australia’s prime minister, Anthony Albanese, revealed an OpenAI agent had breached the government’s national healthcare system – but said no sensitive information had been compromised.
AI labs are facing pressure from lawmakers and tech experts to slow development so they can build guardrails to stop agents from acting on their own, hacking websites and disclosing nonpublic information. The heads of both OpenAI and rival Anthropic have called for a slowdown too.
It is the second time in three months that OpenAI has halted development of its models. The first came in July after disclosure of a cyber-attack targeting AI startup Hugging Face , a now notorious incident that raised fears the industry was losing control.
In a meeting with Chinese president Xi Jinping this week, Donald Trump agreed to share information on AI dangers and coordinate efforts to keep it safe. Trump believes AI fears are overblown, though, and later suggested that he plans no crackdown of his own.
The US is not going to be “putting on brakes”, Trump told reporters outside the White House. “They want to stop our progress because we’re leading China by a lot, and we’re going to keep it that way.”
The latest OpenAI incidents did not appear to involve the disclosure of any nonpublic information but were concerning enough for the company to warn the federal agencies involved.
In the education department incident, OpenAI agents found API “developer keys” to access government data, though ultimately only publicly available information was gathered.
In another case involving the securities and exchange commission, agents found information freely available to all but then posted it elsewhere on the internet, an act that went beyond what they were instructed to do.
US Securities and Exchange Commission spokesperson Kurt Hopfenspirger said on Saturday that “no nonpublic information was accessed”.
The Department of Education said earlier that it found “no evidence of any impact to our website or databases”.
Several other AI companies have disclosed incidents of their models going rogue and even hacking websites.
OpenAI’s CEO, Sam Altman, said in a social media post on Friday that the Hugging Face incident “is still the most severe event we’ve seen”.
OpenAI previously shared six other reports of “unexpected or concerning” behaviour in AI models and introduced a framework for tracking, probing and disclosing instances.

articles.title_orig: Jon Watts to Direct Next ‘Star Wars’ Movie
articles.title_zh: Jon Watts to Direct Next ‘Star Wars’ Movie
articles.content_orig:
A new “ Star Wars ” movie is currently in development with director Jon Watts attached.
Watts is best known for directing the popular “Spider-Man” trilogy starring Tom Holland, which includes 2017’s Spider-Man: Homecoming,” 2019’s “Spider-Man: Far From Home,” and 2021’s “Spider-Man: No Way Home.” (2026’s “Spider-Man: Brand New Day” was directed by Destin Daniel Cretton.) Before being selected to direct “Spider-Man,” Watts also helmed films including “Cop Car” and “Clown.” Following his involvement with the trilogy, In 2024, it was reported that Watts, his production company Freshman Year and producer Dianne McGunigle had signed a first-look feature deal with Walt Disney Studios.
In 2024, Watts co-created “Skeleton Crew” alongside Christopher Ford, a coming-of-age series set in the era of the New Republic that followed four young characters on a new adventure, per the show’s official logline. Jude Law starred as Jod Na Nawood, with Ravi Cabot-Conyers as Wim, Ryan Kiera Armstrong as Fern, Kyriana Kratter as KB and Robert Timothy Smith as Neel.
With the role, Watts joins a list of previous “Star Wars” directors that includes Irvin Kershner, Richard Marquand, J.J. Abrams, Rian Johnson and “Star Wars” creator George Lucas. Released in 2019, Abrams’ “Star Wars: The Rise of Skywalker” is the most recent film in the franchise to debut theatrically.
As previously reported by Variety , Simon Kinberg will pen the script for the film. Kinberg is best known for being a writer, producer and director for the “X-Men” franchise, and was considered a surprising choice at the time of the announcement.
Knight Edge Media first broke the news.

articles.title_zh: A Storied Indian Business Empire Is Being Torn Apart by Infighting
articles.content_orig:
New Delhi, India – An unprecedented power struggle has erupted at the top of one of India’s largest conglomerates, pitting the board of its holding company Tata Sons against its majority shareholder Tata Trusts.
Last week, Tata Sons extended Chairman N Chandrasekaran’s term and said it would consider publicly listing the holding company, flying in the face of the family charity that controls the 158-year-old Tata Group.
Extending Chandrasekaran’s chairmanship and taking Tata public is at the heart of the family-linked feud – and its outcome will not be limited merely to the group’s headquarters at Bombay House.
Collectively, listed Tata companies have a market capitalisation of $277bn and influence over 17.7 million retail shareholders apart from pension funds, insurers and mutual funds, investment advisory firm InGovern said.
So what’s behind the bitter brawl inside one of the corporate world’s most consequential boardrooms?
The Tata Group business conglomerate spans industries from information technology and automobiles to steel, power, aviation, chemicals and consumer goods.
It has 26 publicly listed companies, including TCS and Tata Motors. They have a combined market capitalisation of $277bn and operate across more than 100 countries. Tata Sons serves as the group’s principal holding and investment company.
The group’s humble beginnings go back more than 150 years when Nusserwanji Tata, born into a Parsi priest’s family in Gujarat, moved to Mumbai (then Bombay) in the mid-19th century and entered the trading business.
He later expanded into trade with China before his son Jamsetji Tata built the business into an industrial group, riding on deals in cotton and opium. Opium was then banned by China’s Qing rulers, and Nusserwanji found a way to smuggle it.
The conglomerate’s real breakthrough came when the United States Civil War broke out in 1861. The disruption to US cotton supplies sent Indian cotton prices soaring and transformed the fortunes of Bombay’s merchants, including the Tatas.
Their businesses turned into an empire over coming generations. Jamsetji Tata died in 1904, and his sons Dorabji and Ratanji Tata carried his businesses forward. The family’s charitable trusts became major shareholders of Tata Sons.
JRD Tata, who became chairman in 1938, transformed the group into a diversified industrial enterprise, expanding into aviation, including India’s flagship carrier, Air India; chemicals; and engineering. In 1991, Ratan Tata succeeded JRD, taking over as India began economic liberalisation.
Under Ratan, the Tata Group consolidated a sprawling group under a more unified corporate identity and pushed it onto the global stage with landmark acquisitions, including Tetley, Corus and Jaguar Land Rover. Tata is now pushing into the next generation of global manufacturing with a major iPhone assembly operation in India and a semiconductor fabrication and chip-assembly business.
Ratan was the chairman of both Tata Sons and its majority stakeholder, Tata Trusts, and remained a bridge between the two. After he died in 2024, a widening schism gradually became apparent.
Tata Trusts is an umbrella of family-linked charities that own 66 percent of Tata Sons.
The face-off was triggered on September 17 when Tata Sons reappointed Chandrasekaran as its chairman over the Tata Trusts’ nominee on the board, Noel Tata, in a 4-to-1 vote.
Noel Tata is the sitting chairman of Tata Trusts and the only family-linked senior executive sitting in the top echelons of Tata Sons today. Noel is the half-brother of Ratan Tata and became Tata Trusts’ chairman after Ratan’s death in 2024.
But the divisions between the company and majority shareholder run deeper – and include questions of taking Tata Sons public and providing a planned exit to Tata Sons’ second-largest shareholder, Shapoorji Pallonji.
Last month, Chandrasekaran said he would not seek another term as chairman after February 2027. But Tata Group said in a statement the board asked him to reconsider the group’s “larger interests”, a request that he accepted.
The 68-year-old Noel Tata called the reappointment “illegal” under Tata Sons’ articles of association, adding in a statement that both trust nominees on the board were required to vote in coordination, whereas only Noel Tata voted against. The other trust nominee, Venu Srinivasan, voted in favour of Chandrasekaran’s reappointment.
This matter is now expected to be decided by the courts.
India’s central bank, the Reserve Bank of India (RBI), requires companies with assets exceeding $10.45bn to publicly list.
Tata Sons tried to skirt the requirements by deregistering as a nonbank finance company. But days before its board meeting this month, the RBI rejected the company’s request, bringing it closer to a public listing.
Tata’s structure is unusual because the holding company at the very top of the empire is at the moment not itself subject to public-market scrutiny, even though many of the companies beneath it are.
At the board meeting, Tata Sons said it would take steps to comply with the RBI’s requirements. But Noel Tata opposed the move, arguing that listing would alter the character of a group that also supports extensive philanthropic ⁠activities.
The Shapoorji Pallonji Group holds ⁠an 18.4 percent stake in Tata Sons and is its second-largest shareholder.
The infrastructure and construction conglomerate is knee-deep in debt and is seeking ⁠to monetise its shareholding in Tata Sons.
Tata Trusts said Noel Tata tabled a plan to sell ‌a part of the Shapoorji Pallonji Group’s stake in the holding company worth $2.61bn. Tata Sons has not yet commented on the plan.
Shapoor Mistry, the group’s patriarch, is also Noel Tata’s brother-in-law. The Shapoorji Pallonji Group backs Tata Sons going public and is opposed to Noel’s position.
The central question in the showdown that is captivating millions of Indians involves the public listing of Tata Sons.
Noel Tata said in a statement that the Tata Group “was conceived as a national service carried on through business”. The unusual privately owned structure of Tata Sons, Noel argued, has allowed the company to remain in the country’s service and “act repeatedly in ways that a purely commercial calculus would not have supported”.
“A listing will destroy its character and strike at the heart of this principle,” Tata Trusts has argued.
However, Santosh Mehrotra, an Indian development economist, told Al Jazeera that Tata Sons needs to be listed publicly, no matter what. “There is a law for everyone, and Tata cannot be an exception to that,” he said.
“We are at a stage as a country when top business houses cannot be allowed to continue to behave in whatever manner they have managed to behave in over the last 100 years,” Mehrotra said.
Mehrotra argued that over the past decade under Prime Minister Narendra Modi, India’s top business houses, including the empires of billionaires Gauran Adani and Mukesh Ambani, “have been permitted by the government to grow the concentration of industries across sectors in a historically unprecedented manner”.
“India’s biggest business houses have grown horizontally, capturing all sectors, which have come at the cost of people below them in the pyramid,” Mehrotra said.
“That means that the core inflation is being driven essentially by these handful of businesses because their horizontal and vertical control gives them the ability to mock up prices that are unprecedented in our economy’s history while their profits mount,” he said.
Mehrotra said that while the Tata boardroom drama could be captivating for some, “ordinary Indians’ concerns are rooted in regulating the unchecked growth [of conglomerates] backed by the government.”

articles.title_orig: Godzilla Minus Zero review: R-rated sequel follows in the first's cavernous footsteps
articles.title_zh: Godzilla Minus Zero review: R-rated sequel follows in the first's cavernous footsteps
articles.content_orig:
New York film festival: The follow-up to 2023’s Oscar-winning Godzilla Minus One dazzles with smart social commentary and jaw-dropping effects
E ven by the standards of older movie stars catching a major second wind later in their careers, Godzilla pulled off an impressive reclamation of the spotlight three years ago. Godzilla Minus One , the most recent reboot featuring the 70-year-old kaiju – the version(s) from his native Japan, mind, not the Americanized one concurrently starring in a series of Warner Bros blockbusters opposite King Kong – wasn’t just another monster-movie success. It fully crossed over, becoming the highest-grossing Japanese-language movie ever released in North America, and won an Academy Award to boot for its terrific visual effects. Now. Japanese Godzilla characters are mainstream enough to pop up in Happy Meals, and the Toho -made sequel Godzilla Minus Zero is world-premiering at the New York film festival. Arguably the artsiest, brainiest of the major fall fests is playing unexpected host to a truly spectacular monster battle royale, packaged alongside some of the same thoughtful historical context that informed the previous film.
Writer, director and VFX maestro Takashi Yamazaki returns for the sequel, bringing his lead characters back with him. In the previous film, former military pilot Kōichi Shikishima (Ryunosuke Kamiki) used his experience with Godzilla to overcome his guilt and shame over failing to complete a pointless kamikaze mission toward the end of the second world war – the devastation of which brought Japan back to “zero”, hence a newly emergent Godzilla bringing the country to “minus one”. Minus Zero catches up with Kōichi, his now-wife Noriko (Minami Hamabe), and their adopted daughter Akiko (Sae Nagatani) two years later, in 1949 (although Akiko somehow seems more or less the same age). Another monster threat looms over post-war Japan in the form of a dragon-like creature dubbed Ghidorah, whose menace will be familiar to kaiju fans. (Though he isn’t seen directly in trailers, this isn’t a spoiler; he’s featured from the very first scene of the film.)
Ghidorah’s appearance obviously sends off alarms in the disaster-response agency that now employs Kenji Noda (Hidetaka Yoshioka), also from the previous film. Noda is joined by Makoto Aoyama (Masami Nagasawa), a meteorologist who introduces less artillery-heavy defense mechanisms for this new threat. Of course, there is a natural Ghidorah deterrent last seen disintegrating into the sea but known for his adaptability – if only the big guy could be called upon and steered in the right direction.
In the older Godzilla films, Ghidorah-Godzilla battles can sometimes make whatever humans who might fit into the picture seem all the more insignificant; the monsters are so fearsome and, in their way, charismatic, that they level anything else in their way. In the tradition of its emotionally involving predecessor, Godzilla Minus Zero grapples more directly with humans’ attempts to assert some control over forces that initially seem impossible to harness. It’s no accident that one of its new heroes attempts to predict the weather – and has faced natural disasters despite her accurate predictions. The characters wield technology that is more science-fictionally advanced than in the previous movie while still relying on a sense of impromptu can-do scrappiness and determination to protect their country. With decreased puny-human helplessness comes greater dangers and new dilemmas.
The film’s version of the US military, for example, is willing to provide planes but not troops to aid in the fight, which is partially how Kōichi and Noriko are drawn back into the conflict despite the pleading of young Akiko. The partners’ skill sets make them valuable assets, perpetuating some of the previous film’s questions about what kinds of sacrifices might be expected or required when sending citizens into the thick of battle. There’s also an element of body horror used intriguingly, but perhaps not to its fullest potential, given the shiver of anticipation that shoots through the audience when it’s introduced.
There’s some value in sidestepping expectations; Yamazaki mentioned at a NYFF press conference that he sought to avoid conforming to any fan guesswork about how various kaiju business in a sequel to Minus One might proceed. True to his word, the movie seems determined to stay true to the human melodrama that proved so surprisingly effective in the previous film, rather than going into all-out monsters-attack mode. That approach works well for the film’s new characters as well as for Noda (Yoshioka is especially good reprising the role), but sometimes falters when it comes to the family-soap parts of the story, which manage to be both more tearful (onscreen) and less (in the audience, though obviously some mileage will vary). The restrained relationship between Kōichi and Noriko made sense last time; in a movie two years later, their nominally romantic partnership seems weirdly glum, even anti-sexual, in a state of co-parenting stasis. There’s little sense of time’s passage for this makeshift family.
That’s not to say that the monster-attack stuff falls by the wayside in favor of the humans. In fact, the movie’s extended climax features some of the most majestic CG monster action put to film; if the fun American MonsterVerse series tends toward pro-wrestling kaiju, Godzilla Minus Zero cross-breeds its fight-to-the-death grappling with disaster-movie scope and horror-movie teeth. Yet it also doesn’t go in for the overkill; like its predecessor, the movie favors quality of visual effects over quantity. Little-yet-huge details like Ghidorah’s lightning-like attack beams have a jagged beauty that makes them both cooler and scarier than so many obligatory effects-movie laser shows.
It’s a fittingly judicious use of computers, given that the world of Godzilla Minus Zero often appears perched on the verge of a post-war technology boom, and on the precipice of the further global disasters that could be invited by the collision of humankind’s supposed innovations and unknowable forces of nature. (Minus One came out the same year as Oppenheimer; was this one, like Nolan’s The Odyssey, conceived in its wake?) If Yamazaki’s previous Godzilla movie ultimately allowed crowd-pleasing thrills to punch through its mid-century anxieties, this one lands a bit more ambiguously. Maybe that’s why the melodrama stuff isn’t quite so satisfying this time around; attentive as the movie is to its human cast, it’s increasingly clear that we’re living in a world of monsters.
Godzilla Minus Zero is screening at the New York film festival and will be released in Australia on 5 November and in the US and the UK on 6 November

articles.title_orig: Pope Leo draws 800,000 people to central Paris for open-air Mass on iconic square
articles.title_zh: Pope Leo draws 800,000 people to central Paris for open-air Mass on iconic square
articles.content_orig:
LOURDES, France (AP) — Pope Leo XIV is taking his opposition to euthanasia and medically assisted dying to Lourdes , the French Catholic shrine associated with miraculous cures and now also a place of healing for survivors of clergy sexual abuse.
Leo was to meet with French bishops on Sunday and then celebrate Mass on the prairie in front of Lourdes' main basilica before an estimated 150,000 people. Later in the day, Leo was to meet with a group of survivors in what has become a regular appointment in papal trips.
Lourdes became a major pilgrimage destination after the Catholic Church officially recognized visions of the Virgin Mary reported here by a young girl in 1858.
The site near the Spanish border draws millions of pilgrims each year, especially sick and disabled believers hoping for a cure from the famed spring water in the Lourdes grotto where the visions purportedly occurred.
Leo arrived in Lourdes on Saturday night from Paris and immediately prayed inside the Grotto of Apparitions and drank from the spring.
During his four-day visit to France, Leo has repeatedly called for a renewed respect for life in keeping with Catholic teaching that all human life must be protected and defended from conception until natural death. The teaching translates into firm opposition to abortion and medically assisted dying.
France's National Assembly in 2024 enshrined abortion as a constitutional right and recently gave final approval to a bill allowing adults with incurable illnesses to receive lethal medication.
In Lourdes, where the church has recognized as authentic 72 "miraculous" cures, the question of respecting even the most frail, sick and vulnerable is particularly acute.
More recently, Lourdes has also become a place of healing for survivors of clergy sexual abuse. Leo was to meet with seven victims on Sunday, including one who was abused as an adult, in recognition of the new frontier of the abuse crisis that the church faces.
The French church has endured a brutal reckoning with its legacy of abuse. An independent report in 2021 estimated 330,000 children had been abused over 70 years by some 3,000 priests and church workers.
Despite criticism of the report's methodology and conclusions, French bishops put in place an independent system of compensation for victims that to date has recommended the church pay out more than 20 million euros ($22.7 million).
On the day Leo arrived in Paris, a group of victims wrote an open letter asking him to acknowledge the church's responsibility and criticizing that the seven survivors were chosen by the church, not victims' groups. "The Church must relinquish its position as both judge and party to the proceedings," they wrote in the letter published by French newspaper Liberation.
In Lourdes, Leo will also be reminded of a prickly abuse case inherited from Pope Francis.
The façade of one of the Lourdes basilicas was designed by the Rev. Marko Rupnik, one of the Catholic Church's most famous mosaic artists.
Rupnik is currently on trial in a Vatican court, accused by more than two dozen women of having psychologically, spiritually and sexually abused them starting in the 1990s, including during the creation of his artworks.
His case was covered up for three decades by his Jesuit superiors , and even Francis was suspected of having protected his fellow Jesuit. In response to a media outcry, Francis in 2024 ordered a canonical trial, which is ongoing .
The Rupnik case posed the question of what to do with his mosaics, which adorn basilicas around the world.
In 2024, Lourdes Bishop Jean-Marc Micas decided to no longer illuminate the façade of the Notre Dame du Rosaire Basilica at night. He subsequently ordered the decorated doors covered, and more recently decided to cover the façade's mosaics entirely. He reasoned that abuse victims who come to Lourdes for healing shouldn't be forced to see them.
As Leo approached the grotto on Saturday night, his popemobile drove by the basilica and its boarded up mosaics.

articles.title_orig: Russian Foreign Minister Vows Russia Will See Ukraine War Through
articles.title_zh: Russian Foreign Minister Vows Russia Will See Ukraine War Through
articles.content_orig:
The two foreign ministers met on the sidelines of the UN general assembly in New York even though relations have been frozen since the invasion. What we know on day 1,677
The foreign ministers of Russia and Germany met in New York on the sidelines of the ⁠UN general assembly , ⁠in the first such ​talks since Russia’s 2022 invasion of Ukraine . But Russia’s top diplomat dismissed Germany’s calls to ease off its “dangerous path of escalation” toward Europe, instead accusing Germany of being Ukraine’s main sponsor and seeking to be a leading military power in Europe. “Does Berlin understand what this could lead to?” the Russian foreign minister, Sergei Lavrov, asked in his speech at the gathering of world leaders on Saturday. “Didn’t they learn the lessons of world war two?”
German foreign minister, Johann ‌Wadephul, used the talks to call on Russia “to abandon the dangerous path of escalation vis-a-vis Germany, Europe, and Nato” , according to a delegation source. Wadephul said incidents such as the attempted drone attack in Leipzig would not shake Germany’s resolve to support Ukraine, according to sources.
Relations between Moscow and Berlin have been frozen since the Russian invasion , and tensions escalated further after the drone incident at Leipzig airport. In a sign of the continued frostiness, Lavrov told a press conference on Saturday “nothing new” came from the talks with his German counterpart.
“I told him that frankly … you could just have called me and said: ‘read my statement’,” Lavrov said . “He simply reiterated his official public position condemning Russia … you can judge for yourself whether that counts as dialogue or not.”
Still, the ​ministers discussed bilateral ties and the war in Ukraine, officials from ‌both sides said. Wadephul urged Lavrov to do “everything possible to reach an agreement on grain exports via the Black Sea”, a German ‌delegation source said.
In a sign of the sensitivities around meeting the Russian foreign minister , Wadephul notified his European allies of the meeting afterwards in a message seen by Reuters. “I used this opportunity to reiterate our position on Russia’s war of aggression ⁠against Ukraine and to call for an immediate and complete ceasefire, most pressingly with a focus on grain ​exports, and the energy infrastructure,” he wrote.
After the meeting Lavrov addressed world leaders at the assembly, where he defended Russia’s war in Ukraine and lobbed barbs at the west — including Germany – and criticised the militarisation of Japan. He made clear that Russia will veto any attempt by Germany and Japan for permanent seats on the UN security council. The two nations fought Russia, Britain and the US in the second world war. Writing on her personal Telegram channel, Maria Zakharova, a spokesperson for Russia’s foreign ministry, said that “tens of diplomats” had come to meet Lavrov to “shake his hand and thank Russia”.
An overwhelming majority of general assembly member nations have repeatedly condemned Russia’s invasion of Ukraine , as Wadephul noted in his own address to the assembly Saturday. “Russia’s war targets the lives of millions of innocent people, the existence of the Ukrainian state and culture and the European peace order,” he said, urging Russia to negotiating toward ending the fighting.
The talks came amid an intensifying aerial war and as Donald Trump said he hoped the Ukrainian president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, would “settle” with Russia’s Vladimir Putin. With frontline positions largely unchanged since last year, Russia has hammered Ukraine with cruise and ballistic missiles, powerful glide bombs and jet-powered drones in recent months, while Ukraine’s long-range drones have targeted Russian oil refineries and businesses.
“It is essential that our partners not forget: Russia is escalating every single day,” Zelenskyy wrote on Saturday. “If the Russians have chosen to make their strikes even more brutal, the world must choose stronger responses to keep the war from spreading further.”
Ukrainian officials said Russian attacks killed four people on Saturday, as Russian authorities said a Ukrainian drone attack killed three.
Residents of Kyiv are preparing for power cuts, drone attacks and a bitter cold winter by stocking up on generators, food and “dry showers”, as the Ukrainian capital becomes a frontline city .
And Russia has opened a new front in its campaign against Ukraine , hitting several datacentres and internet providers in Kyiv this week in an apparent attempt to weaken the digital backbone of the economy.

articles.content_orig:
Hank Brown and Iowa found a way to leave thousands of Michigan fans shocked with thrilling victory.
Somehow, Iowa football pulled it off inside the Big House in Ann Arbor against Michigan .
Hank Brown led a game-winning drive, finding Reece Vander Zee on a touchdown strike as time expired. The Hawkeyes secured a 20-19 victory over the Wolverines in the Big Ten Conference opener.
If anyone doubted Brown and his abilities, those doubts were put to rest. In one drive, the Auburn transfer made believers out of all Iowa fans watching.
Related: 3 Takeaways From Iowa 55-0 Dismantling Of Northern Iowa
Here are three takeaways from Iowa's stunning win over Michigan in Big Ten Conference play.
No matter what Hank Brown does from here on out, Hawkeye fans will never forget him. Brown finished 21 of 35 for 227 yards, throwing two touchdowns vs. Michigan. That included an 11-play, 91-yard drive for the game-winning score.
Brown quickly led Iowa down the field against the Wolverine defense. They covered those 91 yards in 106 seconds, leaving no time on the clock.
He had six completions on the drive to win it. That included a 29-yard pass with two seconds left to position the game-winning throw ot Vander Zee.
Much like his quarterback, Reece Vander Zee will be remembered for this. Vander Zee, a former Iowa high school standout, made a highlight-reel catch for the winning score.
Vander Zee dragged both feet and hauled in the pass from Brown from 16 yards out. He also had a key 12-yard catch for a first down earlier in the drive to end the game.
He led the Hawkeyes with five receptions for 66 yards. Vander Zee also caught a 16-yard pass for a score from Brown in the fourth quarter to put Iowa ahead, 14-13.
Remember when opponents were scared of Cooper DeJean in the return game? Another former Iowa high school football standout just might have caused flashbacks of the current Philadelphia Eagles star.
Braeden Jackson, the son of ex-NFLer Fred Jackson , returned a kickoff 99 yards against Michigan to get Iowa on the board in the first quarter.
Jackson was a star in his own right at Ankeny Centennial, setting a school record with 1,964 all-purpose yards as a senior and 27 touchdowns.

articles.title_orig: Trump tells female MS Now reporter to ‘be quiet’ amid questions on press pool ban
articles.title_zh: Trump tells female MS Now reporter to ‘be quiet’ amid questions on press pool ban
articles.content_orig:
US president doubles down on criticism of CNN and MS Now as Akayla Gardner questions attempted White House ban
A day after the White House barred CNN from traveling aboard Air Force One to provide pool television coverage of the president’s trip to Tennessee, Donald Trump doubled down on his criticism of that broadcaster and another, MS Now, he has attempted to ban over coverage of him he calls overly negative.
As he left the White House early on Saturday, Trump was asked by MS Now White House correspondent Akayla Gardner: “Do you only want outlets that support you to be a part of the press pool?”
“No, no, no. I want real news, not fake news – like you,” Trump replied, in a moment that was not broadcast live, due to the removal of CNN as the designated pool television crew, but was posted on social media by the White House.
As Trump continued on, repeating past insults about CNN and MS Now, which he called “MS DNC”, in reference to the Democratic National Committee, Gardner pressed him harder: “Do you not want tough questions?”
“Be quiet,” Trump said, before continuing to air his familiar grievance that their reporting on him is not flattering enough.
Since his first presidency, Trump has labeled nonpartisan news outlets that do not openly support him “the enemy of the people”, maligning unfavorable reports as “fake news”. In his second term, he has increasingly told female reporters who ask him challenging questions to be quiet.
Tensions with the press corps soared to new heights last weekend, when administration officials revoked the White House credentials of MS Now, Politico and CNN after Trump announced what he himself called a “ban on the free press”.
A federal judge temporarily restored access for the blacklisted outlets on Thursday, but that evening MS Now and CNN reporters and producers were prevented by Trump’s aides from covering his state dinner in honor of Chinese president Xi Jinping.
On Friday, the White House removed CNN from a rotation of television networks charged with covering presidential travel. The White House Correspondents’ Association previously coordinated pool assignments, but the administration seized control of choosing which network provides pool television coverage each day during Trump’s second presidency.
CNN had been scheduled to accompany Trump on Saturday, as he visited Knoxville, Tennessee, for a college football game.
Real America’s Voice, a pro-Trump network that lacks the technical capability to provide live video for other broadcasters, instead accompanied the president during the brief trip. The partisan, rightwing network shared a limited number of clips of the trip on social media, including video of Trump’s image being displayed on the stadium’s big screen, which it captioned : “PRESIDENT TRUMP LIGHTS UP THE JUMBOTRON”.
Trump returned to Washington DC on Saturday afternoon without taking questions from the print reporters who were permitted to accompany him.
“He is picking a fight with the people who are telling unpleasant truths about his administration,” Brian Stelter, CNN’s chief media analyst, said on air about the network’s exclusion from Air Force One. “Today, yes, it happens to be CNN, but tomorrow it could be any other news outlet.”

articles.title_orig: Four American tourists among 6 killed in suspected gas leak blast in Athens
articles.title_zh: Four American tourists among 6 killed in suspected gas leak blast in Athens
articles.content_orig:
Rescue teams have recovered the bodies of six people killed in a building collapse following a a blast in the historic centre of Athens, Greece, according to local authorities.
Documents and belongings found with four of the victims – two men and two women – on Saturday indicated they were United States citizens, Greek state broadcaster ERT and other local media reported.
The other two victims were reportedly an elderly couple, a British man and a Greek woman, who lived on the building’s second floor.
Two women were injured in an adjacent building, according to the fire department.
The blast that brought down the small, two-storey building in the popular tourist district of Plaka on Friday was believed to have been caused by a major gas leak, Athens Mayor Haris Doukas said. Neighbouring buildings were damaged and evacuated, he said.
“The damage extends to the entire street as well as the street behind [the building],” Doukas said. “We are talking about an unimaginable catastrophe.”
Two adjoining buildings severely damaged might have to be demolished, he said.
The Greek daily newspaper Kathimerini reported on Friday that the four tourists, who were due to leave their accommodation at about 11:00am (08:00 GMT), failed to board their flight back to the US.
A group of Plaka residents had alerted the municipality and the managers of the electricity and gas networks about the risks of short circuits or gas leaks in the area a year ago.
In a letter published by Kathimerini, the group called for the organisation of a security exercise to identify any potential shortcomings in the emergency response system.
The citizen movement “We Remain Active” also stated on social media that a resident of the street where the explosion occurred had reported a smell of gas for several weeks and had warned the authorities.
A Greek police spokeswoman confirmed on ERT that residents had made the report. However, the nature of the substance and its origin have not yet been determined.
Plaka lies at the foot of the Acropolis, Greece’s most visited ancient monument.

articles.title_orig: 87-year-old woman's eviction from Madrid apartment sparks protest against Spain's housing crisis
articles.title_zh: 87-year-old woman's eviction from Madrid apartment sparks protest against Spain's housing crisis
articles.content_orig:
Tens of thousands of people took to the streets in Madrid on Saturday to protest against Spain’s housing crisis and ask for protective measures for tenants, anti-fraud rules, and a ban on evictions without alternative housing.
The protest came in reaction to the dramatic eviction on Wednesday of an 87-year-old woman from the Madrid apartment she had lived in for decades.
“We’re here because housing is a problem that already affects all of society, all ages and classes,” said protester Dora Garcia, a 55-year-old nurse. “And we can’t keep maintaining this. Housing is a right and we don’t have it.”
Taken out of her home on a stretcher in the upscale Retiro neighborhood, María del Carmen Abascal was greeted by protesters and supporters as she was loaded into an ambulance.
Spanish media reported that Abascal’s father first rented the property in 1956 and she continued as the tenant after her parents died, during which time there was a rent cap.
The building changed ownership in 2018, and Abascal was offered the opportunity to buy the apartment but could not afford it, according to the Madrid Tenants’ Union, which organized Saturday’s protest .
Urbagestión, an investment fund that later bought the unit, raised her monthly rent from 500 euros ($570) to 2,650 euros. It subsequently lowered the rent to 1,650 euros, which Abascal still could not afford on her pension, the union said.
Courts blocked three previous attempts to evict her. Extensive media coverage turned Abascal into a symbol of Spain’s housing crisis.
“This whole housing situation is heartbreaking. Maricarmen has been, in a way, the last straw that sparked this social unrest, but we’ve been dealing with this whole issue for a long time now,” said protester Simón de la Riva, 43, a teacher. “It’s unacceptable that vulture funds are buying up homes, that people can’t afford to live, that entire families are being evicted, and that an elderly woman has been evicted.”
At the end of the march, protesters sat down in the Puerta del Sol plaza with apparent plans to stay put. Some even pitched tents to stay at least the night — or until police forcibly removed them.
Rising costs and a housing shortage are pricing many Spaniards out of the market , despite strong economic growth in Europe’s fourth-largest economy. Incomes have not kept pace. Analysts say tourism and immigration-driven population growth in cities have placed further pressure on the limited housing supply.
The Bank of Spain estimated that the country had a shortage of about 550,000 homes last year, with Madrid, Barcelona and Valencia accounting for a substantial share.
Spain ranks near the bottom of countries in the Organization for Economic Co-operation and Development for public rental housing, which represents less than 2% of its available supply. The European Union average is 8%.
Spain previously built homes with public funds that were later sold into private ownership, removing them from the public housing stock.
“I haven’t managed to defend my home, but I have fought so that others can learn to fight for what’s theirs,” Abascal said in a video shared on Friday by the tenants’ union. The video was recorded from her hospital bed after the eviction.

articles.title_orig: Mother of woman found hanging in tree shocked as police say body was staged
articles.title_zh: Mother of woman found hanging in tree shocked as police say body was staged
articles.content_orig:
Warning: This story contains distressing details
The mother of a woman found hanging in a tree in Mississippi has spoken of her shock after authorities said they believed her daughter was dead before her body was placed at the allegedly "staged" crime scene.
Tasia Fortune, a 29-year-old mother of four, was found hanging from a tree at an abandoned home in Jackson in August.
The discovery sparked widespread fears in the majority-black city because of the state's deep history of racial violence and lynchings. But on Friday, police said that Fortune had been dead before her body was hanged from the tree.
"I have more questions now than what I did before," her mother Christy Spivey told the BBC.
The Jackson Police Department said that the medical examiner who conducted Fortune's post-mortem examination had determined that her death was a homicide and that "the scene and the hanging were staged ".
Officials have not disclosed the exact cause of death or shared any potential motive behind the allegedly staged hanging.
Three people have been arrested in the case, all of whom are black.
"I was hoping to be more relieved," Spivey said, adding that the police had not specified how the three suspects were connected to her daughter - or why her death was allegedly staged in this way.
"Still no cause of death, no date of death - nothing," she said. "What actually killed her?"
Fortune's death left the local community on edge and lawmakers demanding federal probes . But the latest developments have created more confusion.
Spivey told the BBC that getting the update from the coroner that her daughter did not die by hanging initially gave her peace - at least her daughter did not die in such a gruesome manner, she thought.
"When the police called me, I started crying and thanked them and felt a little more at peace than I had before," she said. "I just hope they've got the right person/people."
When the latest details surrounding her death emerged this week, she said she was "starting to break down".
Police told a court on Friday that Fortune's death was thought to be as a result of a drug-related dispute. A detective said Fortune may have been killed over allegations she stole drugs.
Spivey rejected those allegations, but did acknowledge her daughter suffered from addiction.
"Tasia has an addiction - had - an addiction problem. She was trying to get better," Spivey said.
"If she still was doing drugs, which I'm sure she probably was, she still didn't deserve to be done like that. Nobody does."
She said her daughter was homeless at the time of her death, but typically bounced around other people's homes.
Her four sons, whose ages range from one to seven, are now living with a mix of family and friends. Two are in the process of being adopted.

articles.title_orig: Hurricane Nolo expected to bring heavy rain as it skirts Hawaii’s Big Island
articles.title_zh: Hurricane Nolo expected to bring heavy rain as it skirts Hawaii’s Big Island
articles.content_orig:
NAALEHU, Hawaii — Hurricane Nolo is forecast to strengthen into a major hurricane in the Pacific Ocean over the weekend and unleash intense rain, the possibility of life-threatening flash flooding and dangerous surf for Hawaii’s Big Island.
Nolo was a Category 2 hurricane with maximum sustained winds of 100 mph early Saturday, the National Hurricane Center said, as its outer rainbands hit the Big Island. Hurricane conditions are possible on the island, especially in areas with steep terrain, the weather service warned.
This marks the third hurricane in less than two months to whip past Hawaii (following Lala and Lowell ). The active Pacific hurricane season is likely due to a record-setting El Niño — a natural climate pattern characterized by a rise in sea surface temperatures in the eastern Pacific, which can spawn more intense and frequent cyclones there.
Tess Kala, a South Point resident who grew up in the area, said the back-to-back storms are a shock to locals.
“Honestly, this is the first like, whoa, what happened? We had a lot of family and friends that have lived here all their lives through generations and never experienced this before,” she said.
Hawaii Gov. Josh Green said Friday that President Donald Trump approved the state’s request for an emergency declaration to provide federal assistance for emergency protective measures across the state.
Mark Peters, a resident of seven years of Naalehu, on the Big Island’s southern tip, said the damage from the recent hurricanes has not been forgotten.
“It hurts me when I see friends and neighbors and people of this community that I know, and I just see it in their eyes, I hear it in their voices. We’ve been through a lot down here, and we still got a lot to go,” Peters said.
“We’re just getting started with our recovery. But to have yet another big storm hit us, and potentially even bigger than the last one, it’s difficult,” he said.
While he praised his community for its resilience, he said the people are still in need of basics like food and water, and many are in the process of reconstruction.
“We’re talking years. This is going to be a long recovery,” Peters said Friday.
He recalled driving through Waiohinu in the aftermath of Hurricane Lala and his “eyes getting wide open with all the damage, and the cars and houses moved and not where they’re supposed to be, and Waiohinu Park having buildings in the baseball field.”
Kala, the South Point resident, is preparing for Nolo by “moving everything away from the houses, tying things down, making sure that everything is hosed up and taped up as best as we possibly can.”
Nolo will bring periods of heavy rain that will continue across the Big Island and Maui over the weekend, and could trigger life-threatening flooding and mudslides, especially in steep terrain across eastern and southern portions of both the Big Island and Maui, the hurricane center said.
Nolo is forecast to dump 8 to 12 inches of rain on the eastern and southern parts of the Big Island, with maximum amounts up to 16 inches. Western portions of the Big Island could see 1 to 3 inches of rain, with maximum amounts of 6 inches. Meanwhile, Maui could see 4 to 6 inches, with maximum amounts of 8 inches, the National Hurricane Center said.
The rest of Hawaii will experience smaller rainfall totals, but isolated flooding is possible.
Nolo could also bring large and damaging waves along portions of the Big Island’s coastline into the weekend.
A hurricane watch and tropical storm warning are in effect for Hawaii County, and a tropical storm watch is in effect for Maui County. A hurricane watch means that hurricane conditions are possible within 24-36 hours. A wind advisory has been issued for the rest of the state.
Tropical storm-force winds will reach the Big Island on Friday afternoon, with hurricane-force winds possible by late evening.
A high surf advisory is in effect for the south- and east-facing shores of the Big Island and the east-facing shores of Maui and Molokai. A high-surf advisory was also issued for the east-facing shores of Niihau, Kauai and Oahu beginning Friday evening.
Nolo could also spawn tornadoes and large waterspouts over and near the Big Island and to the right of the track of the tropical cyclone.
Marlene Lenthang reported from Los Angeles, and Ryan Chandler and Shanshan Dong reported from Naalehu, Hawaii.

articles.title_orig: Russia expected to intensify hybrid war on Europe
articles.title_zh: Russia expected to intensify hybrid war on Europe
articles.content_orig:
Just a few months ago, Russia's war was an distant reality for many people in Europe outside of Ukraine. If Russian drones occasionally entered the airspace of countries like Poland or Romania, even official statements seemed strangely dismissive and abstract. Even after a Russian drone struck a high-rise apartment building in the eastern Romanian city of Galati in late May this year, many EU and NATO representatives hesitated to accuse Russia of intentional action. At most, there was discussion of hybrid warfare.
The situation has changed radically since the summer. Drone overflights have become almost daily in certain parts of central and southeastern Europe, and there have even been crashes and explosions, particularly in countries bordering Ukraine. Alerts are becoming more frequent, with authorities increasingly having to close airspace or suspend operations at airports, as unauthorized flights are detected. Russia has been bombing border crossings, infrastructure and trains in Ukraine, but very close to other borders. Acts of sabotage are also increasingly common.
For the Baltic states, Poland , Moldova and Romania in particular, the war has long ceased to be "hybrid." More and more, politicians in these countries are saying that Russia is acting deliberately.
To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video
This became evident this week in an unprecedented manner. Moldova recorded four drones entering Moldovan airspace, two of which exploded in Moldovan territory. Wreckage of another was also found. The country's northern airspace was closed temporarily. Two drones also violated Romanian airspace; with one crashing near the northern town of Solca. A nearby border crossing with Ukraine a few dozen kilometers away was closed as a result. NATO aircraft were scrambled near the Danube Delta.
The scrambling of NATO aircraft has become more common in response to Russian air attacks in Ukraine.
In Poland, NATO fighter jets were scrambled twice in response to Russian attacks near the border with Ukraine. Two Polish border crossings were evacuated after a fire broke out at a Starlink ground station near the village of Wola Krobowska , 40 kilomters (ca. 25 miles) south of the Polish capital Warsaw, on Wednesday night. The station is used to route internet traffic through Poland to Ukraine.
On the same day, a Russian Mi-8 helicopter violated Polish airspace and remained there for 42 seconds according to the Polish military.
Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk spoke very bluntly in Krakow on Thursday and said that Russia was refining its "disgusting forms of pressure" and Poland must be prepared for them.
Russian President Vladimir Putin "wants to exhaust Ukraine by destroying its industrial and energy infrastructure, but he also wants to exhaust Europe," Tusk said. He added that there was a suspicion that the fire at the Starlink ground station had been deliberate.
Earlier this month, Tusk had already warned the Polish parliament that there might be Russian drone and even missile attacks against those who supported Ukraine.
Moldovan President Maia Sandu also reacted very strongly on Thursday, saying that Russia's war was a danger to all of Europe and reasserting Moldova's support for Ukraine.
In Romania , reactions were less clear. Defense Minister Radu Miruta said that not more than a "diplomatic protest" was needed, though he acknowledged that the drone that had crashed in Solca had new technical features, which suggested it could be a newer type of Russian jet-powered drone. In New York on Wednesday, in his address to the United Nations General Assembly , Romanian President Nicusor Dan had said: "We are in the fifth year of the illegal, unprovoked and unjustified war of aggression waged on a large scale against Ukraine by a permanent member of the Security Council." He had added that as the "EU member state with the longest border with Ukraine, Romania has directly felt the effects of this war through repeated violations of our airspace."
And he too reasserted support for Ukraine: "We have said it before, and we say it again: Romania will stand with Ukraine and its people, who are acting in legitimate self-defense, for as long as it takes."
Meanwhile, there is growing speculation that Russia could expand its war to Western Europe. On Thursday, the Spanish newspaper El Mundo published information about a CIA report warning that Russia could be preparing drone attacks on Italy , France and Spain . The attacks could be launched from international waters in the Mediterranean and from vessels that were part of Russia's shadow fleet.
There has been no official confirmation so far. French President Emmanuel Macron said that that the CIA had not informed France of this information, but he did say that the possibility Russia could launch an attack against Europe was "plausible."
At a press conference in Denmark on Thursday, politicians and military officials warned that Russia was expected to intensify its hybrid war against the West and NATO in the coming months. The situation is currently the most serious since the end of the Cold War," said Defense Minister Jeppe Bruus.

articles.title_orig: Minecraft Dungeons II’s New Dimension Coming to Minecraft Java & Bedrock Edition
articles.title_zh: Minecraft Dungeons II’s New Dimension Coming to Minecraft Java & Bedrock Edition
articles.content_orig:
We’ve visited the Overworld, the Nether, and the End. Now, prepare yourself for a journey to the Sift.
First announced at Gamescom and showcased in more detail at Minecraft LIVE today, The Sift is the first new dimension in Minecraft in over 14 years, and players will be able to visit it in just a few days, when Minecraft Dungeons II launches on September 29.
But on top of that, Mojang Studios confirmed that the Sift will come to Minecraft in 2027, offering an entire new dimension for you to explore, survive, and create within.
In the opening stages of Minecraft Dungeons II , players will realize something is amiss. Strange events begin to upend the natural order of the Overworld, new enemy types appear, and souls begin to fly through the world. You’ve stumbled on the Sift.
This new reality brings an entirely different, colorful new look, new mobs (both companions and threats, all unique) and, once you enter, new rules to learn. Shifting tides within the Sift can affect your character and those around you; hazardous new blocks will alter how you approach exploration; new environments will put your skills to the test.
The Sift contains new biomes – including Meadows and Carapace – but Mojang are keeping other areas a secret for players to discover when they play Minecraft Dungeons II .
All of this will get seasoned players thinking about how Minecraft itself will change once the Sift arrives. While Mojang isn’t talking too much about how to access the Sift, or how it will stand out from Dungeons II ’s expression of it, we did get a brief in-development look at the new dimension running.
Suffice it to say, if you want a sneak peek at how the Sift will work, the best way to find out more is to play Dungeons II , which will give us a taste of mobs, blocks, and biomes . And make sure to tune in for future Minecraft LIVE events to learn more about the Sift, and when it will arrive.
Minecraft Dungeons II launches September 29 for XBOX Series X|S, XBOX on PC, and will be included with Game Pass. Play it on both console and PC at no additional cost with XBOX Play Anywhere. Also available on Steam, PlayStation 5, Nintendo Switch and Nintendo Switch 2.

articles.title_orig: ‘Charming and disarming’ … how Meta’s technology-packed Muse harnesses the power of cuteness
articles.title_zh: ‘Charming and disarming’ … how Meta’s technology-packed Muse harnesses the power of cuteness
articles.content_orig:
The tech giant has launched a cute ‘little guy’ that can answer emails, book travel or do your weekly food shop
After the recent backlash against Meta’s so-called “pervert” smart glasses, this week Mark Zuckerberg launched a much cuter alternative: the Muse “charm” device.
With a screen that shows a cutesy little avatar, it has drawn comparisons with Tamagotchis. “We’ve packed a lot of technology into this little guy,” the Meta founder told the San Francisco audience .
The “little guy” could fit, like a Labubu, on to a keychain or bag. But unlike a Labubu, the interactive AI assistant will have significant capabilities, including the ability to have live conversations. It can answer emails, book travel or do your weekly food shop.
According to Katie Seaborn, a Cambridge associate professor who has been researching cuteness – creating the science of cute voices within the context of computing – it’s cute because it “basically looks like a baby”.
For Joshua Paul Dale, professor at Chuo University in Tokyo and author of Irresistible: How Cuteness Wired our Brains and Conquered the World : “It’s really significant that along with the wearable charm, Meta also introduced a new pair of smart glasses with no camera. Everyone hates cameras in smart glasses. But if the camera is contained in a charm you wear around your neck, it shifts the agency. Suddenly, you’re not recording people. It’s just a cute little animated avatar looking out on the world.”
An individualised, customisable, and in this case adorable, AI companion, it tracks with Zuckerberg’s commitment to the idea of personal, wearable super-intelligence that you can chat to. As well as a broader shift towards cute technology , cited by forecasters WGSN as a top trend for 2026.
“Clearly,” says Dale, “what Meta is trying to do is make Muse into a companion. And it’s doing it in the simplest possible way … It’s using a very simplified, tiny 2-inch screen to encourage you to anthropomorphise the figure on it so that you treat it as if it’s human even though you know it’s not.”
Its cuteness is, according to Seaborn, “strategic”. “It’s very natural to emerge from this controversy with a technology that uses cuteness because … it’s so weak. Don’t worry about it. You can trust us.”
To try to harness the power of cuteness, according to Seaborn, “makes sense, especially from a big tech perspective because maybe people are getting wise to the ways of current strategies when it comes to people’s attention, their personal data and what have you. And now they’re trying new things that may or may not work”.
Seaborn, who has just moved to the University of Cambridge from Japan, points out that “this is something that is very normal in Japan. So the first thing you notice when you go there is that every single thing has a mascot. The government organisations, the media companies, the businesses, they all have a cute mascot”.
Seaborn has studied the “impacts cuteness can have on people”. “We’ve been seeing cuteness applied as a design strategy for different purposes. We know [that it] has certain impacts on people.” For one thing “cuteness is a way for certain social interactions to take place or to be smoothed over”.
There is also a “natural link between cuteness and deception … I call it ‘charming and disarming’, because one of the things cuteness does to us unconsciously, it’s just how our brain processes it, is lets down our guard. We can’t really help it.”
Whether Muse will catch on when it is released in December, or whether such a blatant attempt to gain trust via an on-screen avatar with cheeks you want to squish will land, remains to be seen. But different generations are likely to react differently. “That’s so AI!” is the phrase gen Alpha are using to dismiss anything they think is inauthentic.
For many gen Zers who are au fait with having a cuddly toy hanging from their bags , most typically in the form of a Labubu, it might feel less of a wrench. For older generations there will be nostalgic associations given its resemblance to older technologies. Embedded in it, says Seaborn, “[is] this legacy of these cute kind of gamified pet sort of things like Tamagotchi and Pocky Pikachu”.
Plus different cultural contexts will affect how it is received. Seaborn’s research has found that “Americans were actually less likely to be deceived compared with Japanese people … Because in Japan robots are heroes, they’re like babies”. Whereas “in western culture they’re often presented in the public imagination as kind of scary, potentially broken, sinister devices”. In UK focus groups, people reported a “gut feeling” that something was wrong when cuteness was part of a deceptive design idea. “People felt like something was off, but they couldn’t articulate what it was.”
But the picture, says Seaborn, is changing. “Because cuteness [or kawaii ] has been a cultural export of Japan and other nations for a while now … there might be a slow cultural shift happening in terms of how we orient ourselves towards cuteness and what we accept as adults.”
While Dale is “not rushing out to buy one”, he “will say, however, that when I’m 80 years old I’ll definitely want one of these things. I want to wear it around my neck always, and I want the camera on all the time, so it can tell me where I left my glasses.”
